The Green-throated sunbird (Chalcomitra rubescens) begins life as a very small altricial nestling; newly hatched chicks weigh approximately 1.33 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.33 grams], a value reflective of the energetic constraints of producing a relatively small egg in a nectarivorous species. This initial wet weight is typical for sunbirds of comparable body size. Eggs are incubated under a thermal regime that averages 34 °C [T = 34 °C], and the incubation period culminates in hatching after precisely 14 days [ab = 14 days]. This relatively short incubation time is consistent with the rapid development observed in many tropical passerines, likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable egg stage. The altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental provisioning during the first days of life.

Upon hatching, the nestling Green-throated sunbird enters a period of rapid somatic growth, fueled by frequent feedings of nectar and small arthropods. Field studies indicate that the fledging stage, marked by the achievement of first flight and nest departure, occurs at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching] under the ambient thermal conditions typical of the breeding season in equatorial Africa (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]). This relatively brief nestling phase is characteristic of small passerines and is thought to minimize the time during which broods are exposed to nest predators. During this period, the developing chick undergoes feather maturation and rapid mass gain, transitioning from a downy, homeothermic-dependent state to a fully feathered fledgling capable of short flights, though it remains reliant on parents for food for several more weeks.

Following the fledging period, the young sunbird progresses through a juvenile stage during which it refines its foraging skills and achieves nutritional independence. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a consistent ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid attainment of sexual maturity is a notable feature of this species' life history, allowing first-year birds to participate in the breeding population relatively quickly, often within the same calendar year as hatching in regions where nectar resources are abundant year-round. The timing of sexual maturation is closely tied to the reliable availability of nectar resources in its tropical forest and savanna habitats. Males and females reach their ultimate adult body masses, which represent the maximum recorded wet weights, with females averaging 10.5 grams [Wwi = 10.5 grams] and males averaging 11.2 grams [Wwi = 11.2 grams], a slight sexual size dimorphism typical in this genus.

In terms of reproductive output, females of the Green-throated sunbird have been documented laying two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and available data suggest they typically produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] when the ambient temperature is approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This annual reproductive strategy, which results in a maximum of four offspring per breeding season, is a common pattern among small Afrotropical nectarivores that time their breeding to coincide with peaks in floral nectar availability. This age at first reproduction is comparable to that of other sunbird species of similar size.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Green-throated sunbird, based on field studies of marked individuals, is approximately 3029.5 days [am = approximately 3029.5 days] at typical ambient temperatures of approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is relatively high for a passerine of its small body size and may be linked to the energetic efficiency afforded by a nectarivorous diet.
